title: Red dye changed wine students' smell words

angle.point: A glass of white wine isn't boring: dye it red and trained wine students describe its smell with the words they used for a real red, because what they see overrides what they smell.
angle.stakes: Frédéric Brochet, working towards a doctorate at Bordeaux's Faculty of Oenology, suspected from experts' tasting notes that a wine's colour steers which smells tasters name; his doctoral work stood on testing it.
angle.turn: A week after the students described a real red and a real white, Brochet gave them that same white twice, one glass dyed red with a grape pigment checked to have no smell, so the only difference was what they could see.
angle.takeaway: The words wine tasters use for a smell can come from the colour they see, shown with one odourless dye and the same white wine in two glasses.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Red dye changed wine students' smell words.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: Frédéric Brochet, working on his doctorate, noticed experts describe smells with things coloured like the wine, and suspected colour chose their words.

elements.text: Smells described with things the colour of the wine

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: He dyed white wine red with grape pigment, and fifty people sniffing both from black glasses smelled no difference. Then he had wine students describe the smell of a red and a white.

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: A week later, he served that same white twice, one glass dyed, so only colour differed.

elements.text: Same white twice: plain, and dyed red

beats.speaker: blink
beats.voiceover: The students generally described the dyed glass with the smell words they'd used for the red.

claims.claim: Oenology students given a white wine dyed red generally described it with the smell words they had used for a red wine; the authors say that, because of what they saw, the tasters discounted what they smelled.
claims.note: Dossier f14, f25, f27. "Fooled" = the authors' finding that visual information made the tasters discount the olfactory information (f27), which they call a real perceptual illusion (f28). The students were not asked the wine's colour; no count of how many. Hook "Red dye changed wine students' smell words" = f25 (dyed white described with the red's smell words).

claims.claim: Frédéric Brochet did the work towards a doctorate at the Faculty of Oenology in Bordeaux.
claims.note: Dossier f4. He is a co-author of the study (f3) with Gil Morrot (first author, INRA Montpellier) and Denis Dubourdieu. Said as "working on his doctorate": the test was part of his doctoral work (f4).

claims.claim: An analysis of four wine experts' tasting notes found that a wine's smells are mostly described with objects that are the colour of the wine.
claims.note: Dossier f5 and f7. The analysis was done by the study's authors, Brochet among them (f3). On screen: "Experts' notes — Smells described with things the colour of the wine". Said as "noticed experts describe smells with things coloured like the wine".

claims.claim: That pattern led the researchers to suspect that a wine's colour directs how its smell is identified.
claims.note: Dossier f8 ("led us to hypothesize that the color of a wine directs the identification of its odor"). "He suspected" = the authors, Brochet among them (f3).

claims.claim: In the first session, oenology students from Bordeaux wrote lists of smell words for a real red wine and a real white wine.
claims.note: Dossier f14 and f17: 54 undergraduates from the Faculty of Oenology of the University of Bordeaux drew up lists of odour descriptors.; "he" = the study's authors, Brochet among them (f3). On screen: "Session 1 — Real red, real white".

claims.claim: One week later, in the second session, the two wines were the same white wine and that white wine dyed red.
claims.note: Dossier f15 and f23 ("The two wines then proposed were W and RW"). "He gave them" = the study's authors, Brochet among them (f3); the paper doesn't say which author served the wine. On screen: "A week later — Same white, one dyed red"; on the ending, the glasses are labelled "Same white wine".

claims.claim: The dye was purified grape anthocyanins, the red pigment of grapes.
claims.note: Dossier f11 (2 g/L of purified grape anthocyanins). Said as "He dyed white wine red with grape pigment".

claims.claim: The dye was checked to have no smell: 50 people compared the dyed and plain white wine in opaque glasses and perceived them as identical.
claims.note: Dossier f12 and f13 (50 people, opaque glasses; "perceived as identical", "the dye can be regarded as having no odor"). Said as "fifty people sniffing both from black glasses smelled no difference"; the check came before the sessions.

claims.claim: In the second session the students generally used the smell words they had used for the real red wine to describe the dyed white wine.
claims.note: Dossier f25: "generally". The paper gives no count of how many did.

publish.title: Red dye changed wine students' smell words
publish.description: Bordeaux wine students described a real red and a real white. A week later they got the same white twice, one glass dyed red with a grape pigment that has no smell, and generally gave it their red-wine smell words. From "The Color of Odors" (Brain and Language, 2001).
